title: India's Maritime Insurance Pool Issues Over 3,000 Cargo-War Policies Within Months Of Launch
text:
Infrastructure
Swarajya Staff
Sep 27, 2026 | Updated 02:01 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
India’s Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool (BMIP) has issued more than 3,000 cargo-war insurance policies within months of its launch, marking an early scale-up of the country’s effort to build domestic capacity for insuring ships and cargo exposed to high-risk maritime routes.
As of 7 September 2026, the pool had issued 3,000 Cargo War policies, 92 Hull War-risk policies and three Protection and Indemnity (P&I) policies, according to a government backgrounder released on Sunday (27 September).
The pool has also ensured uninterrupted availability of war-risk insurance for Indian maritime stakeholders.
BMIP was approved on 18 April and formally launched on 12 May with an underwriting capacity of Rs 13,906.5 crore, or $1.5 billion.
It is backed by a sovereign guarantee of Rs 12,980 crore, equivalent to about $1.4 billion.
The pool provides cover across Hull and Machinery, Cargo, Protection and Indemnity and War Risk categories.
Eligible vessels include Indian-flagged ships, vessels owned, managed or controlled by Indian entities, and cargo vessels either originating from or destined for India.
The mechanism is intended to reduce India’s dependence on foreign maritime insurers, particularly overseas P&I clubs.
Indian shipowners have traditionally relied heavily on international clubs for liability cover, while annual outflows on P&I premiums alone are estimated at $45-60 million.
The pool’s first Hull and Machinery War-risk policy was issued on 12 May to Hoger Offshore and Marine for a vessel operating through conflict-affected waters.
On 30 July, the first P&I policy under BMIP was issued to Shipping Corporation of India by New India Assurance.
Coverage has also extended beyond shipping companies.
Marine Cargo War policies have been issued for industrial cargo linked to Vedanta Sterlite Copper and Balrampur Chini Mills, indicating that the pool is also being used by manufacturers and commodity businesses dependent on maritime trade.
